title: The Taj Mahal
hookLine: Shah Jahan's tomb for Mumtaz Mahal, framed with Qur'an verses

cards: Everything is in pairs. Walk through the great gate and the garden opens in front of you, split by a long channel of water that holds the white dome upside down. Minarets stand at each corner of the platform, matched.
To the left of the tomb, a red sandstone mosque; to the right, a building that copies it exactly, so the view stays balanced. Inside, under the dome, two marble cenotaphs lie side by side.
And that is where the balance breaks. One sits at the exact center. The other is pushed to the side, as if it arrived later and squeezed in.
It did. Today: the Taj Mahal.

teach.b: The Taj Mahal was built by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan as a tomb for his wife, the empress known by the title “Mumtaz Mahal”, who died while he was emperor. The center of the whole design belongs to her.

When Shah Jahan himself died, he was laid beside her, and his tomb is the one off-center, breaking the balance. People call it a monument to love, and it is. But walk closer and the white marble is framed with writing.
Black stone letters set into the marble, framing the arches and the gate: verses from the Qur'an.

teach.h: LETTERS THAT GROW AS THEY CLIMB.
teach.b: The calligrapher, Amanat Khan, signed his work, and the letters are said to grow larger as they climb, so that from the ground they look the same size all the way up.
Among the verses on the great gate, guides point to the end of the surah called al-Fajr, the Dawn.
In Pickthall's translation: "But ah! thou soul at peace! Return unto thy Lord, content in His good pleasure!" And then: enter among My servants, enter My garden.
So a visitor walks through words about a soul returning to God, into a garden with water, toward a grave. The love story is real. But the building also speaks about death, judgment and paradise.
The Taj holds two questions in white stone: how to honor the one you've lost, and where the soul goes next.

how: Muslims pray for the dead and visit graves to remember them; the mosque beside the Taj Mahal is still used for Friday prayer.

games.q: you're Amanat Khan, the calligrapher. your verses run high up the gate, and people read them from the ground. what do you do?
o: make every letter the same size.
make the letters grow larger as they climb.
put the verses only at eye level.
games.why: the letters are said to grow as they climb, so from the ground they look the same size all the way up.

practice: Bring to mind someone you loved who has died, or a love that ended, or a person now far away, and let one ordinary memory come: a voice, a kitchen, a joke.

Just hold them for a minute, the way the garden holds the tomb at its center, and if grief comes, let it. If you pray, you can pray for them, as Muslims pray for their dead; if not, simply say their name.

wordCard.voice: Mumtaz Mahal. The empress for whom Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal in Agra, white marble framed with Qur'an verses about the soul returning to God. Today's word.

orig.note: Persian and Urdu: Taj Mahal, often explained as the crown of the palace.
